passages.happening:
Boaz goes up to the town gate and sits down. The nearer redeemer comes by, and Boaz calls him over to sit (verse 1). Then he gathers ten of the town's elders, and they sit down too (verse 2).

Boaz tells the redeemer that Naomi, back from Moab, is selling the land that belonged to their relative Elimelech. He has the first right to buy it back. If he will not, Boaz is next (verses 3-4). “I will redeem it,” he replied (verse 4).

Then Boaz adds something. “On the day you buy the land from Naomi and also from Ruth the Moabitess, you must also acquire the widow of the deceased in order to raise up the name of the deceased on his inheritance” (verse 5).

The redeemer changes his mind. He cannot redeem it, he says, or he would put his own inheritance at risk. “Take my right of redemption, because I cannot redeem it” (verse 6). In those days, the narrator explains, a man made such a transfer binding by taking off his sandal and giving it to the other (verse 7). So the redeemer takes off his sandal and says to Boaz, “Buy it for yourself” (verse 8).

Boaz tells the elders and all the people that they are witnesses that he has bought all that belonged to Elimelech and his sons, and that he has taken Ruth the Moabitess as his wife, ‘to raise up the name of the deceased through his inheritance, so that his name will not disappear from among his brothers’ (verses 9-10). “We are witnesses,” they answer, and they pray that the LORD will make Ruth like Rachel and Leah, who built up the house of Israel, and Boaz's house like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
The gate of an ancient town was more than a way in. It was a covered space with benches where elders sat, business was done and disputes were heard. It was the town's court and public square. By sitting there and calling ten elders, Boaz holds a formal hearing. Everything is done before witnesses, so that no one can later challenge it.

The legal steps are compressed, but the logic can be followed. Naomi has a right to the family land of her dead husband. The nearest redeemer has the first right, and duty, to buy it so that it stays in the family. At first the relative agrees: adding a field to his holdings is attractive. But Boaz adds that the purchase comes with Ruth, and that any son she bears will carry the dead man's name and inherit the land. The relative would be paying for a field that would pass to another man's line. So he steps aside.

The sandal was a public sign that a right had passed from one man to another, perhaps because setting foot on land was a way of claiming it. The law describes a harsher sandal ceremony for a brother who refuses to marry his brother's widow, and Ruth 4 differs from it in important ways. That is one reason scholars debate how the customs fit together in this story.

The nearer relative is never named. Boaz calls him by a phrase something like so-and-so. The man who would not keep another man's name alive loses his own name in the story.

The Hebrew verb in verses 5 and 10, to acquire, is the verb for the field as well. It is uncomfortable for a modern reader. It belongs to the language of law and contract, and it does not mean that Ruth was property. The whole book says the opposite.

The elders' prayer reaches back to Genesis: to Rachel and Leah, the mothers of the tribes, and to Tamar, another widow whose bold act kept Judah's line alive.
passages.later:
The law of the redeemer and the land stands behind the scene (Leviticus 25:25), and so does the custom of a brother raising up a dead man's name, with its own harsher sandal ceremony, in which the widow was to ‘remove his sandal, spit in his face’ before the elders (Deuteronomy 25:9).

The story the elders recall is told in Genesis 38, where Tamar bears Perez to Judah.
passages.hard:
Deuteronomy 23:3 says that no Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD. How can a Moabite woman marry into Israel and become an ancestor of David?

The tension is real, and the book seems aware of it, since it calls Ruth ‘the Moabitess’ again and again. Readers have answered in several ways.

Later rabbinic tradition held that the law applied to Moabite men and not to women, so Ruth's marriage was lawful. Others note that Ruth had plainly taken Israel's God as her own, and argue that the law shut out Moab as a hostile people, not each foreigner who joined Israel in faith. Many modern scholars read the book as deliberately testing a strict use of the law, holding up a Moabite whose faithfulness puts many Israelites to shame.

These views are not exclusive, and these notes do not choose among them. What is clear is how the book tells it: Ruth's welcome is a gift from the LORD, and she becomes the mother of Israel's royal line.
passages.asks: The nearer relative would not risk his own inheritance, and he is forgotten. Boaz took on the cost, and he is remembered. Ask what it is costing you, or would cost you, to keep someone else's name and future alive. And ask whether you do the good you mean to do openly and with witnesses, or only when it is safe.

passages.happening:
“So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And when he had relations with her, the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son” (verse 13).

The women say to Naomi, “Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a kinsman-redeemer. May his name become famous in Israel” (verse 14). The child will renew her life and care for her in old age, ‘For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth’ (verse 15).

Naomi takes the child, holds him on her lap and cares for him (verse 16). The neighbor women say, “A son has been born to Naomi,” and they name him Obed. ‘He became the father of Jesse, the father of David’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
This is the second of only two places in the book where the narrator says plainly that the LORD acted. In chapter 1 he gave his people food. Here he enables Ruth to conceive. Everything between has happened through ordinary choices and an ordinary harvest.

The women of Bethlehem, who asked in chapter 1 whether this could be Naomi, return to praise the LORD for giving her a redeemer. Here the redeemer is the child, who will carry on the family and care for Naomi in her old age.

Their praise of Ruth is extraordinary in a world that prized sons above everything: she is ‘better to you than seven sons’. Seven was a number of completeness. Ruth's love is worth more than a full house of sons.

Naomi, who said she came home empty, now holds a child in her lap. The book answers her lament not with an argument but with this.

Then the last line turns the family story into Israel's story. Obed is the grandfather of David.
passages.later:
Matthew names this family in the line of Jesus: “Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab, Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, Obed the father of Jesse” (Matthew 1:5).

The book of Samuel tells how the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem was anointed king: “I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have selected from his sons a king for Myself” (1 Samuel 16:1).
passages.asks: Naomi came home empty and ended with a child in her lap, and a daughter-in-law better than seven sons. Ask whom God has given you that you have not yet seen as a gift. And ask whether you can trust him, in your own season of emptiness, to fill what you cannot fill yourself.

passages.happening:
“Now these are the generations of Perez: Perez was the father of Hezron” (verse 18). The list runs on: Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed and Jesse (verses 19-22).

“Obed was the father of Jesse, and Jesse was the father of David” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The book ends with a family line of ten names, from Perez to David. A similar list appears in 1 Chronicles. Perez was the son of Judah by Tamar. Nahshon was the leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness.

The list moves quickly from the time of the patriarchs to David with only ten names. Like many ancient family lines, it seems to choose key names rather than record every generation. Boaz stands seventh in the list, which many readers think is intentional.

The last word of the book is David. A book set in the days when there was no king in Israel ends with the name of Israel's king. The story of two widows, a field and a hearing at the gate was the story of how that king's family began.
passages.later: The same family line is kept in Chronicles: “Boaz was the father of Obed, and Obed was the father of Jesse” (1 Chronicles 2:12). And Luke names the same men in his family line of Jesus: ‘the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz’ (Luke 3:32).
passages.asks: A book of small, faithful acts ends with the name of a king. Ask what small faithfulness of yours might matter to someone generations from now. And think of the names in the list you know nothing about. Ask whether you can be content to be one faithful name among many.
